title: Celts and Romans: from the Helvetii to the Rhine frontier
card: How Celtic peoples lived in today's Switzerland, how Rome conquered them, and how Roman towns, roads and forts shaped the land.

stops.title: The La Tène culture
text: From about 480 BC, archaeologists speak of the La Tène period. It is the later Iron Age. It ends about 30 BC, when the Romans take over.

The name comes from La Tène, a site at the end of Lake Neuchâtel. From 1857, people found many iron weapons and other metal objects there. The 'La Tène culture' means the objects, art and graves of the Celts of this time.

In Switzerland, large cemeteries show how this culture changed. The best known is Münsingen-Rain near Bern, with more than 220 graves. The people of this culture were Celts. Their language belonged to the Celtic family.

stops.title: Celtic peoples and their oppida
text: About 100 BC, several peoples lived in today's Switzerland. The Helvetii lived on the Swiss Plateau, between the Rhine, the Jura, Lake Geneva and the Rhone. The Raurici lived around Basel. Four Celtic tribes lived in the Valais. The Lepontii lived in the Ticino valleys; their language was Celtic. The Raetians lived further east; their core area was the Lower Engadine, South Tyrol and Trentino.
Rome already ruled Geneva (land of the Allobroges) and the south of Ticino (land of the Insubres around Milan).

From the late 2nd century BC, the Celts built oppida. An oppidum is a large place on a hill, protected by a strong wall. Bern-Engehalbinsel was the main oppidum of the Helvetii, with more than 140 hectares. Mont Vully above Lake Murten had a wall 600 m long.

stops.title: The Helvetii leave
text: Orgetorix, a Helvetian noble, convinced his people to move to the Saintonge, in south-west Gaul. In March 58 BC they set out. Caesar says that 368,000 people went, with the Raurici and other groups. Historians think this number is too high. Why they left is not clear. Caesar blames attacks by Germanic peoples.

Caesar says the Helvetii burned about twelve oppida and 400 villages, so that nobody would turn back. At the end of March they met near Geneva. Caesar broke the bridge over the Rhone and did not let them cross the Roman province. So they took the way over the Jura, through the land of the Sequani.

stops.title: Defeat at Bibracte
text: At the Saône river, Roman legions killed the Tigurini, one group of the Helvetii. Talks between the old leader Divico and Caesar failed.

About 20 June, Caesar turned towards Bibracte, a town of his allies the Aedui, to get food. The Helvetii turned and attacked. The battle began about noon and ended at night with their defeat. The battlefield was probably near Montmort, not at Bibracte itself.

Caesar sent the survivors home. He did not want Germanic peoples to settle on the empty Swiss Plateau. According to Caesar, only 110,000 people came back. The Helvetii now probably had a treaty with Rome.

stops.title: Two Roman colonies
text: Rome now planted colonies. A colony was a town of Roman settlers with its own land.

Between 46 and 44 BC, Caesar founded the Colonia Iulia Equestris at Nyon. The first settlers were old soldiers, mostly horsemen. They got land taken from the Helvetii. The colony controlled the way out of the Plateau towards the Rhone valley and Italy.

In 44 BC, the general Lucius Munatius Plancus founded the colony Raurica. Its first place is not known: maybe on the Basel Münsterhügel. Building at Augusta Raurica (Augst) began only about 15–10 BC, when Augustus refounded it. Both colonies spread the Roman way of life.

stops.title: Rome conquers the Alps
text: Emperor Augustus wanted safe roads over the Alps. His stepsons Tiberius and Drusus led the campaign of 15 BC. It was a pincer attack: Tiberius came from Lyon, Drusus marched up the Adige valley, and other troops entered the valleys of Graubünden.
Roman posts at Basel-Münsterhügel and Zürich-Lindenhof, and three watchtowers at Lake Walen, belong to this war. The Lepontii in Ticino and the four tribes of the Valais also surrendered.
A victory monument at La Turbie, above Monaco, built in 7–6 BC, lists the conquered Alpine tribes. Now all of today's Switzerland was under Rome.

stops.title: Legion camp and first provinces
text: After the conquest, Rome set up its first provinces. A province was a territory ruled by a Roman governor. The Helvetii, the Raurici and the two colonies first belonged to Gallia Lugdunensis, then to Gallia Belgica. The mountains – Valais, Leventina and Graubünden – formed one large 'pass province', later called Raetia.

In AD 9 the Romans lost a big battle in Germania. Under Emperor Tiberius they stopped attacking east of the Rhine and guarded the river. At Vindonissa (Windisch), where the Aare, Reuss and Limmat meet, they built a legion camp. About 6,000 soldiers lived there. The legion brought money and work to the region.

stops.title: Claudius: the Valais and its forum
text: Emperor Claudius (41–54) finished the Roman organisation. He reorganised the road over the Great St Bernard. Near the old Celtic village of Octodurus he founded a new town: Forum Claudii Vallensium, today's Martigny.

The four tribes of the Valais were joined into one community, the civitas Vallensium. Its leaders could now become Roman citizens. The Valais left Raetia and, with the Tarentaise, formed the province of the Graian and Poenine Alps. Its governor lived partly in Martigny, partly in Aime in the Tarentaise.
The Great St Bernard was part of the shortest way from northern Italy to the legions on the Rhine. Claudius needed it for his conquest of Britain.

stops.title: Roads and Alpine passes
text: Roman road lists and a Roman road map show the main roads. One road came from the Great St Bernard down the Rhone valley to Geneva. From Vevey a road went to Avenches; from Lausanne one went via Orbe to Besançon. From Avenches the main west–east road ran to Windisch. A branch crossed the Upper Hauenstein to Augst and on to Strasbourg.
In the east, a road came from Bregenz via Chur over two passes to Como and Milan. Roman remains on the Julier pass show that carts used it, but only small two-wheeled carts on steep tracks.
In Roman times the Great St Bernard, not the Gotthard, was the fastest way from the Rhine to Rome. Many visible 'Roman' road tracks are in fact medieval or later.

stops.title: Germania superior and the towns
text: About AD 85, Emperor Domitian created the province of Germania superior (Upper Germany). The lands of the Helvetii and Raurici and the colonies of Nyon and Augst went to it. This lasted until the end of the 3rd century. Eastern Switzerland, Leventina and Graubünden stayed in Raetia. In AD 101 the legion left Vindonissa; the Plateau was now far from the frontier.

This was a time of peace and growing wealth. Aventicum (Avenches), capital of the Helvetii, became a colony about AD 70. Augusta Raurica had perhaps 20,000 people around AD 200. Smaller towns grew at Lousonna (Lausanne-Vidy), Turicum (Zürich, a customs post), Curia (Chur), Genava (Geneva) and Forum Claudii (Martigny).

Central Switzerland (UR, SZ, OW, NW) is left blank: the sources give no province for it here.

stops.title: Alemanni raids, the Rhine again
text: In the 3rd century the empire was in crisis. About 259/260, groups of Alemanni broke through the frontier wall (limes) in south-west Germany and took the land behind it. Rome gave up this land. The Rhine was again the frontier, and the Swiss Plateau was now on the front line.

Emperor Gallienus strengthened Vindonissa. The raids of 260 probably did not reach the Plateau much. But about 275–277, Augusta Raurica and Aventicum were plundered and partly destroyed. Lousonna slowly emptied after the middle of the 3rd century.

layers.name: Alemanni
layers.label: Land behind the old limes, now held by the Alemanni (rough: today's Baden-Württemberg)

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: die nach der Überwindung des obergermanisch-rätischen Limes ca. 259/260 das Dekumatenland kontrollierten

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Völkerwanderung
sources.quote: Die Reichsgrenze wurde an den Rhein zurückverlegt. Das schweizerische Mittelland und die Bündner Alpenpässe befanden sich fortan an vorderster Front.
sources.supports: Rhine frontier, Plateau on the front

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: Der obergermanisch-rätische Limes wurde aufgegeben, sodass erneut der Rhein die Reichsgrenze bildete.
sources.supports: Rome gives up the land; Rhine frontier

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: Gallienus befestigte Vindonissa, doch überfielen die Barbarenheere vermutlich damals das Mittelland nicht

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: Die Kolonien Augst und Avenches wurden wohl erst in den Jahren 275-277 geplündert und teilweise zerstört.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Lousonna
sources.quote: Infolge der Germaneneinfälle entleerte sich die Siedlung ab Mitte des 3. Jahrhunderts n.Chr. allmählich

uncertain: One source dates the destruction of the civil town to 273/274; another gives 275–277.
The Alemanni area is shown as all of Baden-Württemberg, which is only a rough picture of the Dekumatland.

stops.title: The late Roman Rhine frontier
text: Emperors Diocletian (284–305) and Constantine (306–337) rebuilt the defence. They made the provinces smaller: the Plateau now belonged to Maxima Sequanorum; Raetia and Ticino were counted with Italy. New forts stood at Oberwinterthur, Burg near Stein am Rhein (about 294) and Kaiseraugst, where the legio I Martia was based. Inland, walls protected places like Zürich-Lindenhof, Olten, Solothurn and Yverdon.
The Alemanni still attacked; in 352 they burned Kaiseraugst. Under Valentinian I, a chain of stone watchtowers was built along the Rhine; inscriptions date two of them to 371.
About 401, the general Stilicho took the troops away from the Rhine to defend Italy. This did not end Roman rule at once: local Roman institutions went on.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: Letztere wiederum zerfielen in Provinzen, deren territoriale Ausdehnung verkleinert wurde.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: Diokletian und Konstantin (306-337) befestigten auch die Reichsgrenze durch den Bau von Kastellen

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: insbesondere die grosse Festungsanlage des Castrum Rauracense (heute Kaiseraugst), in der die Legio I Martia stationiert war

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Provincia
sources.quote: die aus der Aufteilung der Germania superior entstandene Provinz Maxima Sequanorum , zu der das Mittelland gehörte

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Provincia
sources.quote: Raetia und das Tessin an die Italia Annonaria
sources.supports: Raetia and Ticino in Italia annonaria

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Limes
sources.quote: Kastellen in Zurzach, Kaiseraugst und Arbon und von Befestigungswerken an strategisch bedeutsamen Orten im Hinterland wie Altenburg, Olten, Solothurn, Zürich-Lindenhof, Irgenhausen und Yverdon

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: wie 294 in Oberwinterthur und in Eschenz bei Stein am Rhein

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: setzten sie 352, von Constantius II. im Kampf gegen den Usurpator Magnentius zum Einfall aufgefordert, das Castrum Rauracense in Brand

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Limes
sources.quote: Inschriften belegen den Bau der burgi in Etzgen-Rote Waage und Koblenz-Kleiner Laufen für 371

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Völkerwanderung
sources.quote: das Gebiet der heutigen Schweiz war noch nach 401 Teil des römischen Imperiums
sources.supports: Roman rule did not end in 401

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Römisches Reich
sources.quote: zog jedoch 400 die Truppen von der Rheinfront ab

uncertain: Year of the troop withdrawal: the sources give 400, 401 or 401/402; the text says 'about 401'.
Geneva's late Roman province is not named in the sources used; Geneva is left blank.
Whether late Roman Raetia included all of eastern Switzerland is not checked; drawn roughly.

notes: All areas are built from today's cantons, districts and foreign regions (French départements, Italian provinces, whole German and Austrian states), so ancient borders are only rough. Kinds are used for colour: 'roman' = the main Gaulish province of the Plateau (Belgica, Germania superior, Maxima Sequanorum), 'other' = Raetia, 'ally' = Alpes Graiae et Poeninae, 'noble' = Gallia Narbonensis, 'empire' = Italy; in step 2 'ally' = Raurici, 'noble' = Valais tribes, 'milan' = Lepontii. Negative years are BC.

title: After Rome: Burgundians, Alemanni and Franks
card: How Burgundians, Alemanni and Franks took over from Rome between 443 and the 7th century, and how the west and east of Switzerland grew apart.

stops.title: Burgundians in the Sapaudia
text: In 436 the Huns, probably allied with the Roman general Aëtius, destroyed the first Burgundian kingdom on the middle Rhine. In 443 Aëtius settled the rest of the Burgundians in the Sapaudia as foederati. Foederati were foreign groups that got land and in return had to defend the empire.

Sapaudia means 'land of fir trees'. Later the name became Savoy, but the old Sapaudia was not the same place. Newer research puts it in the area of Geneva, Nyon and Avenches–Windisch, up to the Aare and the Rhine. Aëtius probably wanted to protect the Alpine passes and the Rhine–Rhone route.
The Burgundians were not many. They lived well with the local Gallo-Roman elite, so they left few traces of their own.

layers.name: Sapaudia
layers.label: Sapaudia, where the Burgundians were settled (one modern reading, rough)

places.name: Eburodunum Sapaudiae (Yverdon)
places.note: Base of a Roman lake fleet

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Die Reste der Burgunder wurden 443 von Aëtius in der Sapaudia angesiedelt. Die Namenskontinuität zu Savoyen bedeutet nicht die geografische Identität.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: 436 bereiteten die wohl mit Flavius Aëtius verbündeten Hunnen dem Burgunderreich am Mittelrhein und seinem König Gundahar den Untergang

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Sapaudia
sources.quote: den Raum der drei Civitates Genf (bis zum Zusammenfluss von Ain und Rhone), Nyon und Avenches-Windisch sowie das Gebiet zwischen Aare und Rhein

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Sapaudia
sources.quote: Gall. Name ( Sapa-uidia , "Land der Tannen")

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: als vielmehr die Alpenpässe und die Rhein-Rhone-Verbindung zu sichern

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Völkerwanderung
sources.quote: Sie waren nicht sehr zahlreich, verstanden es aber dank ihrer Politik, mit den lokalen Eliten in gutem Einvernehmen zu leben.
sources.supports: few, good relations with local elites

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Völkerwanderung
sources.quote: indem es ihnen einen Vertrag (foedus) gewährte, der zu ihrer Bezeichnung als foederati führte

uncertain: The location of the Sapaudia is disputed. The coloured area follows the newer reading and is drawn with whole cantons and Bernese districts; the Bernese Oberland is left out without evidence either way.

stops.title: The Burgundian kingdom at its largest
text: The Burgundians soon grew stronger. In 457 they spread south-west into the Rhone–Saône area and in 461 they took Lyon. In 478 a treaty with the Visigoths set their southern border at the Durance river. In the north they pushed the Alemanni out of Langres and Besançon.
When King Chilperic died in 480, the kingdom was at its largest. His sons shared it: Gundobad ruled as high king from Lyon; Godegisel was sub-king in Geneva.
North of the Rhine, the Alemanni were a strong and growing power.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Sie erweiterten 457 ihr Herrschaftsgebiet nach Südwesten in den Rhone-Saône-Raum und besetzten 461 definitiv Lyon.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: 478 wurde die Südgrenze des Reichs am südfranzösischen Fluss Durance durch Vertrag mit den Westgoten festgelegt.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Im Norden verdrängte Chilperich die Alemannen aus Langres und Besançon. Bei seinem Tod (480) hatte das Burgunderreich seine grösste Ausdehnung erreicht.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: dass Gundobad die Herrschaft als Oberkönig mit Sitz in Lyon erhielt, Godegisel, Chilperich II. und Godomar Unterkönige mit den Sitzen in Genf

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: In der Endphase des weströmischen Reiches entwickelten die Alemannen eine grosse Expansionskraft in alle Richtungen

uncertain: The kingdom is drawn with whole French départements; its real borders (especially in the north and west) were different. Whether the Valais already belonged to it in 480 is not clear; it is left blank here.
The Alemanni area is very rough.

stops.title: Franks defeat the Alemanni
text: Clovis, king of the Franks, united the Frankish kingdoms and conquered almost all of Gaul. He beat the Alemanni in 496/497 and again in 506. Their king died, and their independence ended.

The Ostrogothic king Theoderic, who ruled Italy, took the rest of the Alemanni under his protection. Some of them settled in Raetia: around Lake Constance, in the Thurgau and in the Alpine Rhine valley.
The Burgundian kingdom now stood between the Franks in the north and the Goths in the south.

layers.name: Ostrogothic kingdom
layers.label: Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy, with Raetia and protected Alemanni (rough)

layers.name: Franks
layers.label: Frankish rule over the Alemanni north of the Rhine (rough)

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: durch die Siege über die Alemannen (496/497 und 506) die Herrschaft der Franken über fast ganz Gallien

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Chlodwigs zweiter Sieg (506) und der Tod des rex Alamannorum beendeten abrupt die Phase der alemannischen Unabhängigkeit

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: dem Ostgotenkönig Theoderich dem Grossen, der 506 die Reste der geschlagenen Alemannen unter seinen Schutz genommen hatte

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Teile der Alemannen wurden in Oberitalien und offenbar im rätischen Gebiet des Bodenseeraumes, des Thurgaus und des Alpenrheintals angesiedelt

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Ende des 5. Jahrhunderts gerieten die Burgunder zunehmend unter den Druck der Franken im Norden sowie der West- und Ostgoten im Süden.

uncertain: Which parts of today's eastern and central Switzerland were under Ostrogothic control is not clear; the coloured area is a rough guess based on 'Raetia' and the protected Alemanni.
Frankish rule north of the Rhine is drawn as whole Baden-Württemberg and Alsace.

stops.title: Monastery of Saint-Maurice
text: About 380–390, Theodul, the first bishop of the Valais, brought the bones of the soldiers of the Theban Legion to Acaunum. The place became a popular goal for pilgrims.

Between May and June 515, the Burgundian prince Sigismund founded a monastery there. It was consecrated on 22 September. Sigismund had changed from the Arian to the Catholic faith. Monks sang in turns, day and night ('laus perennis'). From the start the abbey was rich in land.
After 515 the cult of Saint Maurice spread far into Gaul. In 516 Sigismund became king.

layers.name: Burgundian kingdom
layers.label: Kingdom of the Burgundians (Swiss part, rough)

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Saint-Maurice (Kloster)
sources.quote: Zwischen Mai und Juni 515 gründete Sigismund, der spätere Burgunderkönig, die Abtei. Die Weihe fand am 22. September

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Saint-Maurice (Kloster)
sources.quote: Gegen 380-390 exhumierte Theodul, erster Bischof des Wallis, bei Vérolliez die Gebeine der Soldaten der Thebäischen Legion

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Saint-Maurice (Kloster)
sources.quote: Mit der laus perennis führte Sigismund einen liturgischen Brauch der Ostkirche ein

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Dieser war zwischen 501/502 und 507 vom Arianismus zum Katholizismus übergetreten

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Saint-Maurice (Kloster)
sources.quote: Von Anfang an war sie reich ausgestattet.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Saint-Maurice (Kloster)
sources.quote: Nach 515 ist der Kult vielerorts zwischen dem Massif central und der Maas nachweisbar.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Als Gundobad 516 starb, folgte ihm sein ältester Sohn Sigismund.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Vallis Poenina
sources.quote: Die in der Sapaudia angesiedelten Burgunder dehnten 457 ihre Herrschaft aus und gründeten 515 das einflussreiche Kloster St. Maurice.

uncertain: Saint-Maurice is often called the oldest monastery in Switzerland still in existence; this is not stated in the quoted source and is left out.

stops.title: The Franks take Burgundy
text: In 522 Sigismund had his own son killed. The Frankish kings used this as a reason to attack. Sigismund was handed over to the Franks and killed.

King Godomar beat the Franks in 524, but in 532 the Franks won near Autun. This was the end of the old Burgundian kingdom. In 534 the Frankish kings shared it. Theudebert of Reims got the north, with Avenches–Windisch and Octodurus (the Valais).
From now on, Burgundy shared the fate of the Frankish kingdom.

layers.name: Ostrogothic kingdom
layers.label: Ostrogothic kingdom with Raetia and protected Alemanni (rough)

layers.name: Frankish kingdom
layers.label: Frankish kingdom, now with former Burgundy (rough)

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: dass Sigismund 522 seinen Sohn Sigerich, den Enkel Theoderichs des Grossen, ermordete

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: Sigismund, der in dem von ihm gegründeten Kloster Saint-Maurice Zuflucht suchen wollte, wurde den Franken ausgeliefert und von König Chlodomer getötet.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: doch unterlag er 532 den erneut angreifenden Franken bei Autun. Dies bedeutete das Ende des altburgundischen Reichs.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: dass Theudebert, der Reimser König, ganz Nordburgund mit Langres, Besançon, Autun und Chalon sowie in der Schweiz Aventicum-Vindonissa und Octodurus erhielt

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Burgunder
sources.quote: In der Folge teilte Burgund das Geschick des Frankenreichs
sources.supports: Burgundy part of the Frankish kingdom

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Vallis Poenina
sources.quote: Nach ihrer Niederlage wurde die V. 534 Teil des Frankenreichs.

uncertain: The battle point is set at the town of Autun; the source only says 'near Autun'.

stops.title: All north of the Alps is Frankish
text: In 536/537 the Ostrogothic king Witigis gave Alemannia and Raetia (Churrätien) to the Franks. Now all the lands north of the Alps in today's Switzerland were under the Frankish Merovingian kings.
The Alemanni kept their name, law and territory. They were ruled by Frankish officials (duces). Raetia also got a Frankish duke later; it protected the passes towards Italy.
Ticino stayed with Italy. From the 6th century, the first Germanic graves south of the Rhine, for example at Basel-Bernerring, Zürich, Bülach and Elgg, are thought to be those of Frankish officials.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: schliesslich wurde das gotische Alemannien 536/537 vom ostgotischen König Witigis den Franken abgetreten

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: die Herrschaft über Alemannien, d.h. über die bisher unter ostgotischem Schutz stehenden Alemannen der Raetia Prima sowie über Churrätien selbst, abtraten

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Die Eingliederung Alemanniens in das Frankenreich beliess den Alemannen den Status einer gens mit eigenem Namen, Recht und Territorium.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: Nach der Eingliederung in das Frankenreich (spätestens um 539) scheint auch in der Raetia ein dux als fränkischer Amtsträger eingesetzt worden zu sein.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Die entsprechenden Gräber in Basel-Bernerring, Zürich-Bäckerstrasse, Bülach und Elgg werden fränkischen Amtsträgern zugeschrieben

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Völkerwanderung
sources.quote: Die Provinz Liguria, zu der die Tessiner Täler gehörten, war schon gegen Ende des 5. Jahrhunderts ins ostgotische Reich integriert worden.

uncertain: Who exactly ruled Ticino between 537 and 568 (Ostrogoths, then East Rome) is only summarised.

stops.title: Two duchies: Burgundy and Alemannia
text: In 561 the Frankish kingdom was divided again. 'Ultrajurania', the Roman-speaking west of Switzerland, went to the Frankish part-kingdom of Burgundy. Alemannia went to Austrasia, the eastern part-kingdom.
The centre of the Alemannic duchy lay south of the High Rhine, in the old Roman settled land. Roman life went on in places like Windisch, Arbon, Oberwinterthur and Zürich.
This line between a Roman-speaking west and an Alemannic east is an early root of the later language border. Its exact course in the 6th century is not known.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: Ultrajuranien, d.h. die romanisch geprägte Westschweiz, fiel an Burgund, Alemannien ( Schwaben ) mit den östlichen Alpenvorlanden an Austrasien

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Bis ins 7. Jahrhundert lag der Machtschwerpunkt der von den Merowingern ein- oder abgesetzten alemannischen Herzöge südlich des Hochrheins

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: romanische Kontinuitätsinseln vorhanden waren, wie zum Beispiel in Windisch, Eschenz, Arbon, Bregenz, Oberwinterthur oder Zürich

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: Als Grenzschutz gegen die Langobarden erlangte Churrätien für die fränkische Italienpolitik erhöhte Bedeutung.

uncertain: The border between Ultrajurania and Alemannia is drawn with today's cantons and Bernese districts; the real 6th-century border is not known.
The link to the later language border is an interpretation, not a quote.

stops.title: Alemanni settle south of the Rhine
text: Before the 6th century, Germanic groups south of the Rhine were few and isolated. Larger Alemannic settlement came late, under the Frankish kingdom. From the second quarter of the 7th century, finds show stronger links with the Alemannic lands north of the Rhine. More settlements appear, also because Alemanni moved in.
Place names show the steps. Older names end in -ingen; later ones in -ikon or -inghofen; the latest in -wil or -wiler.
In the Roman-speaking west, people kept their Latin-based (Romance) speech.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Erst vom zweiten Viertel des 7. Jahrhunderts an werden die Einflüsse aus dem rechtsrheinischen alemannischen Kernland stärker.

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Die globale Zunahme von Fundstellen bezeugt einen Siedlungsausbau im 7. Jahrhundert, der nicht nur auf Bevölkerungswachstum, sondern auch auf Zuwanderung von Alemannen

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: eine alemannische Siedlungsbewegung grösseren Ausmasses relativ spät anzusetzen, jedenfalls erst im politischen Rahmen des merowingischen Frankenreichs

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: ist eine ältere Namenschicht (Formen: -ingen-, -heim- und -dorf) von den Namen eines ersten frühmittelalterlichen Ausbauraums (Haupttyp: -inghofen bzw. -ighofen, ikofen sowie -ikon)

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: und denjenigen eines zweiten Ausbauraums (Formen: -wil und -wiler) zu unterscheiden

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Frankenreich
sources.quote: Ultrajuranien, d.h. die romanisch geprägte Westschweiz

sources.title: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (HLS): Alemannen
sources.quote: Germanische/alemannische Einsprengsel hat es als isolierte Erscheinungen links des Rheins vom 4./5. Jahrhundert an gegeben

uncertain: The coloured areas only show the rough political frame; Alemannic settlement in the 7th century did not yet cover all of it (especially the Alps).
That the west kept its Romance speech is supported only by the phrase 'romanisch geprägte Westschweiz' (for 561).

notes: All areas are rough and built from today's cantons, districts and foreign regions (whole French départements, Italian provinces, German and Austrian states). Kinds used for colour: 'burgundians' = Burgundian kingdom, 'france' = Frankish kingdom, 'burgundy' = Frankish part-kingdom of Burgundy (Ultrajurania), 'alemanni' = Alemanni, 'other' = Ostrogothic/Italian rule, 'noble' = Churrätien.
